Semantic HTML & Page Architecture

Choose a semantic element or a generic container

Use div to group content for styling and span to mark an inline phrase for styling when no specific element fits. Use a semantic element when the content has a clear purpose. For example, nav identifies major navigation and helps assistive technology expose it as a landmark.

How to try it In index.html, replace the content between <body> and </body> with this example. Save the file and reload it in the browser.

<div class="site-bar">
  <span class="brand">City Workshop</span>
  <nav aria-label="Main"><a href="#sessions">Find sessions</a></nav>
</div>
<h2 id="sessions">Sessions</h2>

What to expect The nav has a navigation role. The outer div groups it with the brand.

Structure a page with seven semantic elements

A page-level header introduces the site, nav holds major links, and main wraps the dominant content. Use section for a thematic group, article for a self-contained item, aside for related material, and footer for closing details. Landmark roles depend on context. For example, a header inside an article is the article’s header, whereas a page-level header is the banner. A named section can be exposed as a region.

How to try it In index.html, replace the content between <body> and </body> with this example. Save the file and reload it in the browser.

<header>
  <h1>City Workshop News</h1>
  <nav aria-label="Main"><a href="#updates">Updates</a></nav>
</header>
<main>
  <section id="updates" aria-labelledby="updates-title">
    <h2 id="updates-title">Latest updates</h2>
    <article><h3>New weekend sessions</h3><p>Registration opens next week.</p></article>
  </section>
  <aside><h2>Related information</h2><p>Bring a notebook.</p></aside>
</main>
<footer><p>Contact the workshop team.</p></footer>

What to expect Inspect main and the named Updates region in the accessibility tree.

Decide between section, article, and div

Ask what the block represents. If the block would make sense when published on its own, it can be an article. If it groups one topic within the page, use a section with a heading. If it only creates a styling wrapper, use a div.

How to try it In index.html, replace the content between <body> and </body> with this example. Save the file and reload it in the browser.

<section>
  <h2>Events this month</h2>
  <div class="event-grid">
    <article><h3>Build a Portfolio</h3><p>Starts June 12 at North Hall.</p></article>
    <article><h3>Learn Web Forms</h3><p>Starts June 19 at North Hall.</p></article>
  </div>
</section>

What to expect Each event can be read independently. Both belong to Events this month.

Recognize block and inline layout

In normal flow, a block box starts on a new line and generally stretches across its container. An inline box flows with surrounding text. CSS display changes layout while the HTML element retains its meaning. A span styled as a block is still a span.

How to try it In index.html, replace the content between <body> and </body> with this example. Save the file and reload it in the browser.

<div style="background:#e9f1f7">This div starts on its own line.</div>
<p>Read this <span style="background:#ffe9a8">highlighted phrase</span> in the same line.</p>
<p>Now <span style="display:block;background:#ffe9a8">this span starts on a new line.</span></p>

What to expect Compare the two spans. Only the last one starts a new line.

Hands-on exercise

Refactor a div-only news page. Give it a header, nav, main, two articles in a titled section, a related-links aside, and a footer. Inspect the page landmarks in DevTools.
